sources.publisher: Embassy of the Democratic Republic of the Congo in the Netherlands
sources.title: Country history and president’s biography: birth, family and 2019 assumption of office
sources.findings: Read the embassy page’s relevant late-history and presidential biography sections. It confirms the full name, birth on 13 June 1963 in Kinshasa, father Étienne’s opposition/prime-minister background, the 30 December 2018 vote and 24 January 2019 assumption of office. This concerns the Democratic Republic of the Congo, not the neighbouring Republic of the Congo. Its official election narrative is supplemented by independent reporting on the dispute. The historical five-year mandate wording is not a current assertion that only one term has occurred. Earlier country-history sections were not comprehensively fact-checked or copied.

sources.title: 31 March 2018: UDPS leadership election and presidential nomination
sources.findings: Read VOA Afrique’s AFP report dated 31 March 2018. It confirms his election as UDPS leader and nomination as presidential candidate at the congress ending overnight Friday–Saturday, with father Étienne’s February 2017 death as background. Party nomination is not a national election victory. The planned 23 December polling date later changed; use the independently confirmed actual 30 December election. The article’s unqualified Belgian marketing/communication diploma statement is not adopted because later reporting flags its disputed validity and no academic record was inspected. Its broad party-name variant is normalised to Union pour la démocratie et le progrès social.

sources.title: 2023 campaign profile: family exile, 2011 parliamentary seat refusal and contested governing record
sources.findings: Read Africanews/AFP’s profile for the 2023 re-election campaign. The URL and narrative place it before the 20 December 2023 vote even though the page shows an August 2024 modification date; do not redate the campaign. It supports family exile in Belgium as a young adult and winning a Mbuji-Mayi seat in 2011 while refusing to sit. Election is not continuous parliamentary service. The marketing/communication credential is explicitly disputed, so no verified earned degree is claimed. Free primary education is presented as a government-claimed achievement, not an independently audited outcome. Political opposition arrests and a mixed record are contextual assessments; an ally’s corruption case is not Tshisekedi’s personal conviction.

sources.title: 24 January 2019: inauguration, disputed election and denials of a backroom deal
sources.findings: Read Reuters’s 24 January 2019 inauguration report on Investing.com. It establishes actual succession to Kabila, peaceful handover, the 30 December election, the court’s rejection of Fayulu’s complaints, Church tally-based objections and both camps’ denials of a backroom arrangement. Court confirmation of the official result does not eliminate the documented dispute; allegations from sources or opponents are not adopted as proven personal fraud. Kabila was the outgoing president, not an opposing candidate personally defeated in that election. Aspirations in inaugural remarks are not already achieved results.

sources.title: 6 December 2020: coalition termination and conditional threat to dissolve parliament
sources.findings: Read VOA’s 6 December 2020 account of the televised speech. He ended the FCC–CACH coalition and sought a new absolute majority through an informateur. The URL misleadingly says he dissolved the Assembly, but the headline and body make dissolution conditional on failure to build a new majority. Ending the coalition is not the same as forming the replacement cabinet that day or terminating all political influence of Kabila. The stated need for change is his justification, not an independent evaluation of every predecessor policy.

sources.title: 6 February 2021: Tshisekedi assumes the rotating AU chairmanship
sources.findings: Read the AU’s 6 February 2021 press-release PDF. It confirms the election and actual handover from Cyril Ramaphosa at the 34th Assembly, with Tshisekedi present physically and Ramaphosa participating remotely. The 2021 rotating AU chair is distinct from the AU Commission chair, Moussa Faki Mahamat, named separately in the release. Do not substitute the 2020 selection in anticipation for the 2021 start date. Summaries of outgoing Ramaphosa’s pandemic programmes are not all credited to Tshisekedi.

sources.title: 5 February 2022: Macky Sall succeeds Tshisekedi as AU chair
sources.findings: Read the AU’s 5 February 2022 handover PDF. It explicitly ends Tshisekedi’s 2021 chairmanship that day and installs Macky Sall. This prevents extending the role indefinitely or calling him current AU chair in 2026. Political praise and achievement claims in the ceremony are not independently measured programme outcomes, and AU chairmanship does not imply chairmanship of the permanent Commission.

sources.publisher: Presidency of the Democratic Republic of the Congo
sources.title: 20 January 2024: second-term inauguration and policy pledges
sources.findings: Read the presidency’s article and date, 20 January 2024, recording the second-term oath before the Constitutional Court at Martyrs Stadium. Its phrase au lendemain de sa réélection is a general after-the-election expression, not proof that the election occurred the previous day. Jobs, purchasing power, security, diversification and public-service promises are prospective commitments. Audience counts and celebratory assessments are not independently verified. Dynamic November 2026 sidebar items are not part of the January inauguration chronology.

sources.title: 20 January 2024: second inauguration, observer criticism and electoral commission response
sources.findings: Read Reuters’s 20 January 2024 second-inauguration report. It records the opposition’s rejection, CENCO criticism of serious irregularities, the CENI position that infractions did not affect the outcome, and dismissal of official court challenges. Major challengers themselves declined to use the courts, so do not assert that each named opposition leader filed and lost a case. Actual office-holding and a disputed electoral mandate can both be recorded. No exact vote percentage, polling-station audit or contemporary poverty estimate is carried into the dossier.

sources.publisher: United States Department of State declaration, archived by PA-X
sources.title: 4 December 2025: DRC–Rwanda joint declaration establishing the Washington Accords
sources.findings: Read the PA-X record’s description and extracted text of its archived four-page State Department declaration. It dates the signing to 4 December 2025 and identifies Tshisekedi and Kagame with Trump as witness. The declaration reaffirms the 27 June peace agreement and 25 April principles, and groups these with regional economic integration arrangements as the Washington Accords. The PDF print timestamp of 5 December is not the signature date. Mining, infrastructure and other investment opportunities and return of displaced people are aims, not completed investments or returns. No handwritten signatures or all underlying agreements were separately audited.

sources.title: 4 December 2025: leaders affirm commitments while fighting continues; separate M23 talks
sources.findings: Read Reuters’s 4 December 2025 signing report on Investing.com. It confirms the ceremony amid continued fighting, previous June commitments, regional economic integration, and the separate Qatar-mediated M23 track. M23 was not present at the Washington meeting; its statements are not the DRC–Rwanda declaration itself. UN experts’ assessments, Rwanda’s denial and allegations from combatants remain distinct. A critical-minerals agreement described as due to be signed is not independently treated as completed solely on this article. This historical report does not establish exact battlefield conditions in November 2026.

sources.title: 11 November 2026: referendum law promulgated on 9 November
sources.findings: Read Anadolu’s 11 November 2026 account of Law 26/045, promulgated 9 November, with its reported 10 November broadcast. The law provides a referendum framework for a new constitution or changes; it is not an already approved constitution or an already completed third presidential term. The legal interpretation and procedural details are news reporting, not an independently reviewed original law or court decision. Opposition concern and the presidential camp’s popular-sovereignty justification are attributed. Exact projected term-end dates and the minimum-petition provisions are not necessary to the profile and were omitted.

sources.title: 11 November 2026: new referendum law, third-term controversy and no announced referendum date
sources.findings: Read Reuters’s 11 November 2026 report syndicated on AOL after the direct Reuters URL proved unavailable. It corroborates Monday 9 November signing and Tuesday announcement, records third-term fears and his denial coupled with conditional willingness, and explicitly says no referendum date had been announced. That dated absence is not a guarantee that nothing changed after 11 November. His May warning that the 2028 vote might be delayed by war is not an enacted postponement. A potential change to protected constitutional limits is not proof that those limits had already been abolished.

sources.title: 14 November 2026: completed arrival in Phnom Penh ahead of the Francophonie summit
sources.findings: Read ACP’s 14 November 2026 report citing the presidency’s confirmation that he had arrived in Phnom Penh that day. Completed arrival provides recent personal-activity evidence. The 15–16 November summit, prospective bilateral meetings and secretary-general selection were future events from that article’s standpoint and are not declared completed on that evidence. Willingness to withdraw Juliana Lumumba’s candidacy is not a verified election outcome. Distinguish Cambodia arrival from the earlier Antalya visit and the different Republic of the Congo visited in early November.

portraitReview.unresolved: Read cropped Commons record, full parent record and official State Department Flickr page. The 560×724 crop was uploaded by Sashi Suseshi on 13 February 2026; parent 3000×2053 file by RandomUserGuy1738 on 4 February 2026. Flickr and EXIF give capture/upload on 4 February 2026, whereas the caption says 4 February 2025; this date discrepancy remains unresolved. Commons parent title/description incorrectly abbreviates the country as Republic of Congo, while the current Flickr title identifies Democratic Republic of Congo. Neither the country error nor the unrelated French caption sourd is adopted as biographical evidence. Photographer Freddie Everett is identified in the official caption and EXIF; uploaders are not substituted as photographers. Flickr marks United States government work and the parent records FlickreviewR 2 confirmation on 4 February 2026; Commons applies the U.S. federal-work public-domain basis, not a CC BY copyright licence. Original crop request on 18 November returned curl 22, HTTP 403 and reported HTTP 000; referenced cached JPEG is absent. No pixels viewed: identity, original colour, crop correspondence, resolution suitability and the conflicting capture year require further review.
